gloss_terse: to growl (as a lion devouring prey) or groan (in suffering or anguish)
gloss_readable: A vivid sound-word that captures two distinct registers of deep, guttural vocalization. When predators are in view, it denotes the low, rumbling growl of a lion over its prey — distinct from the roar (shaag) of the initial attack. Isaiah deploys it twice to portray Assyria's terrifying advance (Isa 5:29-30). In human contexts, it shifts to the groan of one in physical or emotional anguish, as in the regretful sufferer of Proverbs 5:11 and the silent mourners of Ezekiel 24:23.

senses.1: The deep, sustained growl of a lion while feeding on its kill, distinct from the attacking roar. Spanish 'bramará' and 'ruge' capture the bestial rumble well. Used figuratively of Assyria as a devouring lion in Isaiah 5:29-30 and of a wicked ruler in Proverbs 28:15.
senses.2: A groan of suffering, distress, or bitter regret uttered by a human being. English glosses 'you-shall-groan' and Spanish 'gimas' reflect anguished vocalization. In Proverbs 5:11 the wayward man groans as his flesh wastes away; in Ezekiel 24:23 the exiles groan silently in their iniquities rather than mourning openly.

gloss_terse: to dedicate or consecrate oneself; to separate for sacred purposes or in apostasy
gloss_readable: This Niphal form carries the reflexive force of setting oneself apart for a sacred purpose — or, tragically, for an unholy one. At Hosea 9:10 Israel 'consecrated themselves' to the shameful Baal, while in Ezekiel 14:7 the apostate 'separates himself' from the Lord. Leviticus 22:2 and 15:31 use the same root for priestly separation from holy things to avoid profanation. The multilingual evidence — Spanish 'apartaréis' and English 'separates-himself' — underscores the reflexive, volitional nature of the act.

senses.1: To dedicate or devote oneself to a deity or sacred purpose, whether legitimate or idolatrous. At Hosea 9:10 Israel consecrated themselves to Baal-peor; Spanish 'consagrándome' and English 'consecrated-themselves' preserve the reflexive devotional force. Zechariah 7:3 uses the infinitive absolute for ritual abstinence in a fasting context.
senses.2: To separate oneself from the holy or from God, expressing apostasy or ritual distance. Ezekiel 14:7 describes one who separates from the LORD and sets up idols; Leviticus 22:2 commands priests to hold sacredly aloof from holy offerings. Spanish 'apartaréis' and English 'separates-himself' highlight the volitional withdrawal.

gloss_terse: to live as a Nazirite; to take or observe a vow of consecrated abstinence
gloss_readable: Exclusively found in Numbers 6, this Hiphil denominative from nazir describes the formal act of undertaking or maintaining a Nazirite vow. The vow involves abstaining from wine and grape products, avoiding contact with the dead, and letting the hair grow uncut. Spanish 'separarse' and 'separará' capture the core idea of setting oneself apart, while the repeated phrase 'to the LORD' in the Hebrew anchors every use in devoted service to God.

senses.1: To undertake or maintain a Nazirite vow of consecrated abstinence before the LORD. All five occurrences appear in the Nazirite legislation of Numbers 6. The vow entails separation from wine (Num 6:3), uncut hair (6:5), and corpse impurity (6:6). Spanish 'para separarse' and 'se separará' convey the self-imposed discipline, while 'to the LORD' (lYHWH) marks the devotional orientation of each instance (6:2, 5, 6, 12).

gloss_terse: we (first-person plural pronoun, abbreviated form of anachnu)
gloss_readable: An abbreviated form of the standard first-person plural pronoun anachnu ('we'). It appears sparingly in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in direct speech that carries emotional weight — Joseph's brothers protesting their innocence (Gen 42:11), Israel grumbling against Moses in the wilderness (Exod 16:7-8), the Reubenites pledging to cross the Jordan armed (Num 32:32), and the communal confession of Lamentations 3:42. Cognate forms appear in Arabic (nahnu), Ethiopic, and Aramaic.

senses.1: First-person plural personal pronoun 'we,' functioning identically to anachnu but in a shorter, possibly older or dialectal form. Spanish 'nosotros' and French 'nous' render it straightforwardly. Its five occurrences all appear in emotionally charged direct speech: collective self-identification (Gen 42:11), complaint (Exod 16:7-8), military pledge (Num 32:32), and penitential confession (Lam 3:42).

gloss_terse: Nahath — name of an Edomite clan leader, a Levite, and a temple overseer under Hezekiah
gloss_readable: A personal name borne by three distinct individuals in the Old Testament. The earliest is a grandson of Esau through Reuel, listed among the Edomite clan chiefs (Gen 36:13, 17; 1 Chr 1:37). A second Nahath appears in the Levitical genealogy as a descendant of Elkanah (1 Chr 6:26), likely a variant of Tohu/Toah. The third served as a temple overseer managing contributions and tithes during Hezekiah's reforms (2 Chr 31:13). The Septuagint renders the name variously as Nachoth, Nacheth, and Naath.

senses.1: Nahath son of Reuel, grandson of Esau, an Edomite clan chief. Listed in the Edomite genealogies at Genesis 36:13, 17 and 1 Chronicles 1:37. The Septuagint renders the name as Nachoth or Nacheth. Spanish 'Najat' preserves the guttural opening consonant.
senses.2: Nahath the Levite, a descendant of Elkanah appearing in 1 Chronicles 6:26. Likely a textual variant of Tohu (1 Sam 1:1) or Toah (1 Chr 6:19). The LXX reads Kainath here, suggesting early scribal confusion.
senses.3: Nahath the overseer, one of the Levitical officials appointed by King Hezekiah to manage temple tithes and contributions (2 Chr 31:13). The Septuagint A-text reads Naeth, distinguishing this figure from the earlier bearers of the name.

gloss_terse: riches, wealth, possessions; treasures (probably an Assyrian/Aramaic loanword)
gloss_readable: A term for accumulated wealth and material possessions, appearing only in the plural (nekasim). Likely borrowed from Akkadian nikasu ('property, gain'), it carries a slightly formal, even exotic flavor in Hebrew. It often appears alongside osher ('riches') and kavod ('honor'), as in Solomon's request (2 Chr 1:11-12) and the Teacher's lament over wealth one cannot enjoy (Eccl 5:19; 6:2). Joshua 22:8 uses it for the livestock and spoil the Transjordan tribes carried home.

senses.1: Material wealth, riches, and possessions viewed as accumulated property. Spanish 'bienes' and French 'possessions' capture the tangible, inventory-like quality. Frequently paired with osher and kavod to form a triad of prosperity (2 Chr 1:11-12; Eccl 6:2). In Ecclesiastes 5:19 God grants nekasim as a gift to be enjoyed; in Joshua 22:8 the term denotes cattle, silver, gold, and spoil distributed among the eastern tribes.

gloss_terse: Nimshi — grandfather (or ancestor) of King Jehu of Israel
gloss_readable: The name of Jehu's grandfather (or more distant ancestor), consistently used in the patronymic formula 'Jehu son of Nimshi.' This identifying phrase appears across the narratives of Elijah's commission to anoint Jehu (1 Kgs 19:16), Jehu's revolt and anointing (2 Kgs 9:2, 14, 20), and the Chronicler's account of Ahaziah's death (2 Chr 22:7). The Septuagint renders it Namesthei or Namessei. The name may derive from the root m-sh-h ('to draw out').

senses.1: Nimshi, the ancestor of King Jehu, used exclusively in the patronymic 'Jehu son of Nimshi.' All five occurrences serve as a fixed identifying formula across both Kings and Chronicles. Spanish 'Nimsi' and French 'Nimshi' preserve the form. The designation links Jehu's dynasty to a recognized clan lineage, from Elijah's prophetic commission (1 Kgs 19:16) through the coup narrative (2 Kgs 9:2, 14, 20).

gloss_terse: flowing honey, honey dripping from the comb; used figuratively of sweet words or kisses
gloss_readable: Designates honey in its most naturally appealing form — fresh, dripping straight from the comb. French 'miel vierge' ('virgin honey') and 'rayon de miel' ('honeycomb') beautifully capture the unprocessed purity implied. The word appears in wisdom literature as a standard of sweetness: God's judgments are sweeter than nopheth (Ps 19:10), and the full person spurns it (Prov 27:7). It also serves as a potent figure for dangerously seductive speech (Prov 5:3) and the beloved's honeyed lips (Song 4:11).

senses.1: Literal flowing honey or honey dripping naturally from the comb, representing the finest quality of sweetness. French 'miel vierge' and Spanish 'panal' highlight the unprocessed, comb-fresh character. Psalm 19:10 pairs it with devash as a superlative comparison for the sweetness of God's ordinances. Proverbs 24:13 commends it as good, while Proverbs 27:7 notes that even nopheth is loathsome to the sated.
senses.2: Figurative sweetness applied to speech or kisses, often with an undertone of danger or delight. In Proverbs 5:3 the lips of the forbidden woman drip nopheth — enticing but deadly. In Song of Solomon 4:11 the lover's lips drip nopheth alongside honey and milk, evoking intimate sensory pleasure. The image trades on the literal sense to invest words and touch with irresistible allure.

gloss_terse: to strike down, ensnare, lay a snare; to trap or entangle someone
gloss_readable: Originally meaning 'to knock or strike' (cf. Aramaic nqash, 'to strike'), this verb specializes in Hebrew as a figure for ensnaring — bringing someone down the way a hunter brings down a bird with a thrown stick. Spanish 'atrape con lazo' ('catch with a snare') and French 'prendre au piege' ('catch in a trap') capture the hunting imagery well. It appears in warnings against idolatrous entanglement (Deut 12:30), in psalmists' descriptions of enemies laying traps (Ps 38:12; 109:11), and in the ironic reversal where the wicked are caught in their own net (Ps 9:16).

senses.1: To lay a snare or set a trap for someone, actively plotting their downfall. Spanish 'ponen trampas' and French 'prendre au piege' convey the deliberate, predatory intent. Psalm 38:12 describes enemies who 'lay snares' while the psalmist is afflicted; Psalm 109:11 envisions a creditor ensnaring all the wicked man's goods. Deuteronomy 12:30 warns Israel not to be ensnared by pagan worship practices.
senses.2: To be caught, ensnared, or entangled — the passive or reflexive result of a trap springing shut. English 'is snared' and Spanish 'fue enlazado' mark the completed entrapment. In 1 Samuel 28:9 Saul's inquiry about the medium implies a trap being set for the woman's life. Psalm 9:16 celebrates divine justice: the nations sink in the pit they made, their own foot caught in the net they hid.

gloss_terse: to unfasten, loosen, set free; to release bonds or prisoners
gloss_readable: A Hiphil verb meaning to loose what is bound — whether physical fetters, yoke-thongs, or a person held captive. Isaiah 58:6 pairs it with 'break every yoke' in the great fast-day oracle, calling for the loosening of bonds of wickedness. The psalmist celebrates God as the one who 'sets prisoners free' (Ps 146:7) and who sent word to release Joseph from chains (Ps 105:20). Job 6:9 uses it figuratively: 'that he would let loose his hand and cut me off.' Spanish 'desatar' and 'soltando' vividly express the unshackling force of the word.

senses.1: To unfasten or loosen physical restraints such as thongs, yoke-straps, or bonds of wickedness. Isaiah 58:6 commands loosening (hatter) the thongs of the yoke as part of true fasting. French 'secouer' ('to shake off') and Spanish 'desatar' ('to untie') capture the breaking of physical constraints. The emphasis is on the material bonds rather than the person bound.
senses.2: To set free or release a person from captivity or imprisonment. Psalm 105:20 recounts how Pharaoh sent and released Joseph; Psalm 146:7 praises the LORD who sets prisoners free. Spanish 'soltando' ('releasing') highlights the liberation of persons. Job 6:9 extends the image metaphorically: Job wishes God would 'let loose his hand' — release restraint — and finish him off, a striking inversion of the liberation motif.
